DEAR MAYO CLINIC: I was told that my pancreatic cancer can't be removed with surgery because the tumor involves nearby blood vessels. Are there other treatment options, and could surgery become possible later?
ANSWER: Being told that pancreatic cancer is inoperable can be difficult to hear. But "inoperable" can describe different situations, and understanding why surgery wasn't recommended is important.
What does inoperable pancreatic cancer mean?
In some cases, the cancer has spread, or metastasized, to other locations outside the pancreas, and surgery can't remove all the disease. In other cases, the cancer hasn't spread to other organs, but the tumor has grown outside the pancreas and involves nearby veins or arteries. These tumors may be completely removable with surgery, or they may be locally advanced pancreatic cancer, which occurs in up to one-third of all patients at diagnosis.
In the past, patients whose tumors involved critical blood vessels weren't offered surgery because of the complexity of these operations. Today, more effective chemotherapy and radiation treatments, along with advances in surgical techniques, allow more complex operations to be considered for some select patients.
That doesn't mean every person who has been told that surgery isn't an option will eventually be able to have an operation. If you've been told your tumor can't be removed because it involves major blood vessels, it's important to get another opinion from a center that has extensive experience evaluating and treating complex pancreatic cancer to help ensure all appropriate treatment options have been considered.
Determining whether pancreatic cancer can be removed involves more than looking at a single scan. Considerations include:
Whether the cancer has spread to other organs.
Where the tumor is located.
How it involves nearby blood vessels.
Whether the cancer can be completely removed.
Whether the person is healthy enough to tolerate a major operation.
The risks and benefits of an aggressive approach.
Can treatment make surgery possible?
How the cancer responds to treatment also can provide important information.
In the past, a patient was operated on first, then given chemotherapy after surgery. Increasingly, chemotherapy is given before surgery. Pancreatic cancer can spread at a microscopic level that can't be seen on imaging. Chemotherapy can treat cancer cells that may not be visible. Giving treatment first also allows for assessment to determine if the cancer is responding.
People whose cancers respond to treatment may be better candidates for surgery. That response also can help the care team plan for larger and more complex operations for some patients whose tumors initially were considered inoperable.
For that reason, surgical candidacy may change over the course of treatment rather than being determined only by a scan at diagnosis.
Blood vessel involvement can make pancreatic cancer surgery considerably more complex, but it doesn't necessarily mean the same thing for every patient.
In selected patients, surgery may include removing and reconstructing an involved vein, artery, or both, or even multiple vessels. These operations aren't appropriate for everyone and require careful patient selection and extensive surgical experience.
The goal isn't to perform an operation simply because it technically can be done. The care team has to determine whether surgery, combined with other treatments, offers a meaningful benefit for that person. That means considering:
The extent of the cancer.
How it has responded to treatment.
Risks and complexity of surgery.
A person's overall health.
The potential to prolong life and improve the quality of life.
When should you seek a second opinion?
Ultimately, it's important to get a second opinion when diagnosed with pancreatic cancer. Pancreatic cancer treatment has changed significantly in recent years, and there may be more options available than people realize.
A second opinion doesn't mean another surgeon will recommend an operation. Another evaluation may confirm that the treatment plan you've already received is the right one. But particularly when surgery is ruled out because the tumor involves critical blood vessels, evaluation at a surgical center with extensive experience treating pancreatic cancer can help ensure that all appropriate options have been considered.
A few factors to determine may be:
Why surgery has been ruled out.
Whether the cancer has spread to other organs.
If the concern is involvement of critical blood vessels.
Whether chemotherapy should be given first.
If surgery could be reconsidered depending on how the cancer responds.
People should understand not only what treatment is being recommended but why. If you've been told that pancreatic cancer is inoperable, an additional expert evaluation can help you understand your options and determine the treatment approach that is most appropriate for you.
Mark Truty, M.D., Hepatobiliary and Pancreas Surgical Oncology, Mayo Clinic, Rochester, Minnesota

The post Arizona boy faces rare oral cancer with help from proton beam therapy close to home appeared first on Mayo Clinic News Network. ]]> When Jake Garcia was 7 years old, a routine visit to the dentist led to a diagnosis his family never expected: a rare oral cancer.
Jake would need surgery, chemotherapy and radiation therapy. Through a collaboration between Mayo Clinic and Phoenix Children's Hospital, Jake received proton beam therapy at Mayo Clinic, home to Arizona's only proton beam therapy program.
Watch: Jakey's story
Journalists: Broadcast-quality video (2:31) is in the downloads at the end of this post. Please courtesy: "Mayo Clinic News Network." Read the script.
Proton beam therapy delivers radiation directly to a tumor while reducing radiation exposure to surrounding healthy tissue, a precision that is especially important for children.
"For pediatric cancers, we strongly favor proton beam for almost any site simply because of that principle of reducing overall exposure to radiotherapy in a developing child, where we want to cure the cancer while avoiding potential longer-term developmental side effects or risks of other cancers in the future," says Dr. Jonathan Ashman, medical director of the Proton Beam Therapy Program at Mayo Clinic in Arizona.
The benefits extend beyond pediatric care; in a study published in The Lancet, Dr. Samir Patel, a radiation oncologist, and investigators found that patients with head and neck cancers can live longer with fewer side effects if treated with proton beam radiation therapy.
Jake and his twin sister, Ella Garcia
Cancer affects more than the patient.
Throughout his cancer journey, his family worked to preserve as much normalcy as possible for Jake and his twin sister, Ella. Having proton beam therapy available in Phoenix allowed the family to stay close to home during treatment and maintain important routines.
Mayo Clinic's Child Life team also helped Jake and Ella navigate an experience that could be frightening and unfamiliar. For Jake, comfort sometimes came in the form of Seaweed, his stuffed turtle, who accompanied him to treatment. Seaweed even inspired the ocean scene painted on Jake's radiation mask.
Elizabeth Hardin, child life specialist, with Jake
Ella faced the experience alongside her twin brother. A child life specialist helped her better understand why Jake needed treatment and what was happening to him, an important part of supporting the entire family through a child's cancer diagnosis.
Jake also held onto the things he loved. He continued drawing and creating comics and kept up with karate during his cancer journey.
Today, he is back in school, spending time with friends, drawing and just earned his black belt in karate.
Jake, Ella and part of his care team at Mayo Clinic in Arizona

ROCHESTER, Minn. — Mayo Clinic researchers, in a study published in Nature Communications, have identified a group of BRCA2 gene variants associated with a moderate risk of breast cancer, a finding that could help healthcare teams better assess a person's cancer risk and personalize care.
The researchers studied 70 BRCA2 gene variants, that they labeled as hypomorphic variants because they only partially disrupt BRCA2 function. They examined how these variants affect the way BRCA2 works and analyzed genetic testing data from a large number of people who had undergone hereditary cancer testing.
Researchers within the study note that individuals who inherit these specific gene changes are estimated to have a 20% to 25% lifetime risk of developing breast cancer. By comparison, people with more common harmful BRCA2 variants may have a 50% to 70% lifetime risk. Because of this reduced risk, these variants are also labeled as reduced penetrance pathogenic variants.
Fergus Couch, Ph.D.
"This shows that not all harmful BRCA2 variants carry the same level of breast cancer risk," says Fergus Couch, Ph.D., a breast cancer researcher at Mayo Clinic Comprehensive Cancer Center. "Understanding these differences could help us better match cancer prevention and screening strategies to an individual's actual risk."
The findings have potential implications for cancer screening and prevention. The researchers note that people who carry these variants may still qualify for and benefit from regular mammograms and breast MRI. However, a more precise understanding of risk could be important when patients and their healthcare teams consider risk-reducing surgery.
"A small subset of breast cancers are likely caused by BRCA2 hypomorphs," says Dr. Couch. "Women and men who inherit these variants should benefit from risk management strategies tailored to the level of risk associated with the specific variant."
The researchers also examined whether tumors associated with these variants may be sensitive to PARP inhibitors, a class of targeted cancer drugs that interfere with the ability of cancer cells to repair damaged DNA.
Their findings suggest that some of the tumors associated with hypomorphic BRCA2 variants may respond to PARP inhibitors. Tumor testing may help determine whether this type of treatment is appropriate for an individual patient.
The researchers are continuing to identify and characterize hypomorphic variants in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes associated with inherited breast cancer risk.
"Once the hypomorphic variants are all identified, we will be able to better define risk management and therapeutic strategies for those who carry these variants," Dr. Couch says.
The research was conducted in collaboration with investigators from Ambry Genetics. For a full list of funding, disclosures and contributing authors, see the study.

The post Ultrarunner races again after stomach removal surgery to prevent cancer appeared first on Mayo Clinic News Network. ]]> Michelle raced the Ultra Tour Monte Rosa, which is a 63-kilometer (about 39-mile) race through the Swiss Alps, 11 months after surgery to remove her stomach.
On Sept. 5, 2026, Michelle Young raced about 39 miles through the Swiss Alps, with more than 12,000 feet of elevation gain and loss during the Ultra Tour Monte Rosa. It was her third time racing in the Swiss Alps — but her first without a stomach.
Just 11 months earlier, Michelle underwent robotic-assisted surgery at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, to remove her stomach because of a rare hereditary cancer syndrome. She had been told that after surgery, she probably would not be able to compete in ultrarunning again.
The discovery that would change Michelle's life began almost by chance.
Michelle, an oncology clinical trials manager in Minnesota, mentioned to a oncologist colleague that her father and cousin had died of stomach cancer, both in their 40s.
The colleague suggested Michelle, 53, get a screening endoscopy, a test that can detect abnormal areas or polyps in the stomach. Michelle requested the test in March 2025, at the same time as her routine colonoscopy.
"Thank God I did that test," says Michelle. She learned her stomach was covered with precancerous polyps.
"I was devastated," she says. "I wanted to get a second opinion, which brought me to Mayo Clinic."
Genetic testing identifies a rare syndrome
At Mayo Clinic, Michelle met Travis Grotz, M.D., a surgical oncologist, and Lisa Boardman, M.D., a gastroenterologist. Given Michelle's family history, her care team recommended genetic testing.
The testing showed that Michelle had gastric adenocarcinoma and proximal polyposis of the stomach, or GAPPS, a rare hereditary cancer syndrome that substantially increases the risk of stomach cancer.
"We recommend removal of the stomach, or a gastrectomy, to prevent stomach cancer because we do not reliably know which polyps will become cancer," says Dr. Grotz.
During a total gastrectomy, the surgeon removes the entire stomach and connects the esophagus to the small intestine, allowing food to continue through the digestive tract. Without the stomach serving as a food reservoir, patients need to eat smaller, more frequent meals.
"Patients tend to lose weight and struggle to maintain muscle mass," says Dr. Grotz. "They can also experience abdominal cramping, nausea, diarrhea and bloating."
For an ultrarunner like Michelle, the challenge would be to consume enough calories to sustain her endurance training and avoid debilitating symptoms.
Dr. Grotz and Michelle discussed her options extensively.
"I had to think, what if I don't get my stomach removed and I get gastric cancer? I have two daughters. I want to be here for them," says Michelle.
In September 2025, Michelle raced in the grueling Barkley Fall Classic 50K, a roughly 31-mile trail race in Tennessee, what she thought would be her final ultra event. Then she prepared for surgery.
Surgical reconstruction helps preserve endurance
"Michelle was an intense ultramarathon athlete, which presented a unique challenge when thinking about life after gastrectomy," says Dr. Grotz. "But I knew we could help by creating a stomach-like pouch from her intestine, called a J-pouch."
On Oct. 13, 2025, Dr. Grotz performed a total gastrectomy and created a jejunal J-pouch using part of Michelle's small intestine. He folded a segment of the jejunum into a J shape and connected it to itself, creating a reservoir before connecting it to the esophagus.
J-pouch after a total gastrectomy
"This restores some capacity for patients to eat larger meals and have more normal function in eating than if they did not have the J-pouch," says Dr. Grotz.
Within four weeks of surgery, Michelle returned to running. By six weeks, she was lifting weights and increasing her running mileage.
"I just started doing what I've always been doing, but I felt like I had to relearn to eat," says Michelle. "I was chewing my food thoroughly, almost grinding it, before swallowing, and not drinking 30 minutes before or after I ate."
Michelle kicked off her trial running season in April 2026 with a 20-mile race in Wisconsin, followed in July by a 26.2-mile race on the rugged Superior Hiking Trail in Duluth, Minnesota.
Returning to the trails
Michelle raced the Moose Mountain Marathon in Lutsen, Minnesota, in September 2026, finishing within 5 minutes of her personal record.
Michelle now follows a structured fueling plan for her endurance events, eating and drinking at regular intervals to maintain her energy. Consuming enough calories remains a challenge.
Dr. Grotz says he has never had another patient compete at Michelle's ultrarunning level — distances greater than 26.2 miles — and is learning from her experiences.
"In Switzerland, I stood on the top of the mountain, amazed that I made it," she says.
A week after returning home from Switzerland, Michelle ran the Superior Fall Moose Mountain Marathon in Lutsen, Minnesota, finishing within 5 minutes of her personal record.
"Mayo Clinic was my saving grace," she says. Next year, Michelle plans to tackle the Barkley Fall Classic 50K once again.

DEAR MAYO CLINIC: My spouse has been diagnosed with liver cancer. We're wondering what kind of treatment she may need and how her doctors will determine that.
ANSWER: Liver cancer can be hard to detect because there often isn't pain or other symptoms. Treatment decisions are often complex and require a multidisciplinary team. Liver health and cancer characteristics are key to choosing the most effective treatments.
The liver is an organ about the size of a football and serves a vital role, including:
Filtering and detoxifying harmful substances.
Processing and storing nutrients.
Producing proteins, clotting factors and bile, which helps remove waste and digest fats.
Regulating metabolism.
Guarding against infection.
While alcohol, smoking, obesity, diabetes, high blood pressure and cholesterol, diet, and genetics can contribute to liver cancer, the leading cause worldwide is hepatitis B and C.
The main type of liver cancer is hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
HCC starts in the liver cells. Factors for determining what treatments will be most effective include:
Stage of the cancer.
Health of the liver and why it became unhealthy.
Number and size of the tumors and if they have metastasized.
The care team guiding treatment decisions may include a hepatologist, who specializes in liver disease, as well as surgeons, medical and radiation oncologists, and interventional radiologists. There are many potential treatments available, particularly for people with earlier-stage disease. Determining which is appropriate requires considering the whole picture.
Liver cancer is staged differently from many other cancers. HCC can be assigned the familiar stages of 1 through 4. More often, another system that accounts for liver health is used. The Barcelona criteria (BCLC) stages cancer at 0, A, B, C and D. Many patients are already at stage B when they're diagnosed but can have a good treatment outlook. Cancers at stage C typically can't be cured. Patients with stage D disease may be best served with treatments based on symptoms, not the tumor.
Imaging plays an important role in diagnosis and determining the best treatment plan. HCC can often be diagnosed without a biopsy. Specialists who regularly evaluate liver imaging can help determine which treatment options make the most sense for each patient.
For someone with a well-functioning liver and a small tumor, treatment to destroy or remove the tumor is often an option. High-quality imaging helps pinpoint the tumor's size and location. This information helps the care team choose the least invasive treatment that will effectively treat the cancer while preserving as much healthy liver tissue as possible.
Surgery used to be routinely recommended for tumors smaller than 2 centimeters. However, ablation, or inserting a small needle into the tumor to burn it, often can provide the same result as surgery.
Preserving as much of a healthy liver as possible is particularly important because it doesn't regenerate in the way people may imagine. For instance, if the right side of the liver is removed, the structures lost don't grow back. Instead, the remaining liver tissue grows larger.
When removing a tumor, we need to ensure the amount of liver left behind is enough for the person to live with. For someone with a healthy liver, about 25% of their liver may be enough. For someone with liver disease or concerns about liver function, about 40% is needed.
For some patients, we can use highly selective treatments that deliver medication or radiation beads through an artery supplying the tumor. These approaches destroy the tumor or slow its growth while limiting damage to the rest of the liver.
If someone has poor liver function but has a tumor or tumors that meet the appropriate criteria, a liver transplant may be an option. Transplant is considered the gold standard for curing liver cancer. After recovery, well-selected patients can expect a long and relatively normal life.
In more advanced disease, treatment may have a different goal. The cancer may not be cured, but treatment can help someone live longer or more comfortably. Medical oncologists can also help shrink liver tumors using systemic treatments such as immunotherapy or targeted therapy.
Particularly with early-stage liver cancer, it's essential to determine whether there are ongoing causes of liver damage that can be eliminated. For example, if a liver is unhealthy due to alcohol abuse, some damage can be undone, or the liver can recover to some degree when someone stops drinking. In patients who suffer from liver damage related to metabolic associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), dietary and lifestyle changes and even some medications may help reduce risks and liver injury.
Patients with a possible liver tumor should talk with their healthcare team about all treatment options and seek care at a center that regularly treats liver disease and liver cancer.
Susanne Warner, M.D., Hepatobiliary and Pancreas Surgical Oncology, Mayo Clinic Comprehensive Cancer Center, Rochester, Minnesota

ROCHESTER, Minn. — Sometimes innovation in cancer care means developing something entirely new. Other times, it means returning to an old idea with the knowledge and tools to make it work better.
Both are happening in stomach cancer surgery, says Travis Grotz, M.D., a Mayo Clinic surgical oncologist who specializes in treating stomach cancer.
Travis Grotz, M.D.
From adapting a surgical pouch used in colorectal surgery to revisiting an operation largely abandoned decades ago, surgeons are finding new ways to treat stomach cancer while focusing on how patients will eat, recover and live after surgery.
At the same time, Dr. Grotz says the disease itself is changing. Stomach cancers in the U.S. are increasingly being diagnosed in younger people and in different parts of the stomach than they were decades ago.
Here are several changes Dr. Grotz says patients should know about.
An old stomach cancer operation is getting a second look
For cancers in the upper portion of the stomach, surgeons once commonly performed a proximal gastrectomy, removing the upper portion of the stomach and reconnecting the remaining stomach directly to the esophagus.
The operation could effectively treat the cancer, but there was a significant problem: Patients often experienced severe bile reflux after surgery.
"The patients' quality of life was negatively impacted," Dr. Grotz says.
Eventually, surgeons in the U.S. largely moved away from the procedure and instead removed the entire stomach.
Now, an approach being performed is a technique called double-tract reconstruction and Mayo Clinic surgeons are using it to change how the remaining stomach, esophagus and intestine are connected, helping preserve part of the stomach while reducing reflux. Mayo Clinic surgeons have adapted that approach for the more advanced stomach cancers typically seen in the U.S.
The result is an approach that allows surgeons, for appropriate patients, to remove enough tissue to treat the cancer while preserving part of the stomach. Dr. Grotz says the incidence of reflux with the reconstruction can be around 5%.
A lesson from colorectal surgery may help patients eat more normally
Removing the entire stomach can treat cancer, but it also eliminates the body's reservoir for food. Without a stomach, patients typically need to eat five or six small meals throughout the day and can experience "dumping syndrome," in which food moves too rapidly into the small intestine.
Surgeons are adopting a concept familiar in colorectal surgery: modifying the small intestine to create a J-pouch, a new reservoir that helps do the job the stomach did.
"The pouch holds on to the food for about 90 minutes, and then it slowly releases it," Dr. Grotz says.
That can make a substantial difference in everyday life. Dr. Grotz estimates more than 80% of patients with a pouch can return to eating roughly three normal-sized meals a day.
"You really wouldn't even know they have it when you're eating," he says. "They may eat a little slow but definitely still within the realm of normal."
The goal goes beyond successful surgery. It is to help patients return to a full and meaningful life afterward.
Stomach cancer found early may not require traditional surgery
Most stomach cancers in the U.S. are discovered after they have advanced, but patients whose cancers are found early may have another option.
Some can be treated through an endoscope rather than conventional surgery. The procedure requires specialized expertise and allows physicians to remove the cancer through an endoscope without removing the stomach.
That expertise can matter when patients are considering where to seek care, Dr. Grotz says. A patient who might be offered a larger operation elsewhere could, after careful evaluation, be eligible for endoscopic treatment at a center with the necessary experience.
For patients who need surgery, minimally invasive and robotic approaches also can reduce the physical burden of treatment.
For most patients with locally advanced stomach cancer, treatment involves more than an operation. Chemotherapy, immunotherapy and surgery increasingly work together, with the sequence tailored to the individual patient.
Even some patients whose cancer has spread beyond the stomach may be considered for surgery after responding well to systemic treatment.
"Surgery is a great consolidative therapy," Dr. Grotz says. "If you've had a great induction response to therapy, then it's very effective to consolidate with surgery and get rid of the rest of the cancer."
Stomach cancer is increasingly affecting younger people
The profile of stomach cancer in the U.S. also has changed.
Decades ago, Dr. Grotz says, stomach cancer more often occurred in the lower portion of the stomach and in older patients. Today, physicians are seeing more proximal and diffuse stomach cancers, including cancers in younger adults.
Researchers are trying to understand why.
One area Dr. Grotz and colleagues are studying is whether greater consumption of ultraprocessed foods could be contributing to the increase in early-onset stomach cancer. Dr. Grotz cautions that current evidence shows an association, not proof that these foods cause stomach cancer. Researchers are using large datasets and artificial intelligence to investigate those relationships further.
Dr. Grotz says the question deserves particular attention because today's younger adults have been exposed to ultraprocessed foods much earlier in life than previous generations were.
"What we eat is going to affect our stomach; it's the first place it goes," he says.
Innovation can mean doing more ... and sometimes doing less
Taken together, the advances reflect a broader change in how surgeons approach stomach cancer treatment.
The goal is not simply to perform the largest possible operation. Depending on the cancer and its stage, treatment may mean removing a tumor endoscopically, preserving part of the stomach, creating a new reservoir after the stomach is removed, or combining surgery with increasingly sophisticated systemic and regional treatments.
Sometimes progress also comes from looking backward.
The return of proximal gastrectomy is one example: an operation surgeons knew could treat cancer but largely abandoned because of its side effects. Surgeons are now revisiting it with an approach designed to address the problem that led them to move away from the procedure.
For patients, Dr. Grotz says, those advances can translate into something deceptively simple: treating the cancer while preserving as much normal life as possible.
Dr. Grotz is available for interviews about the latest developments in stomach cancer treatment and research.

PHOENIX — Radiation therapy is sometimes needed after mastectomy and breast reconstruction for breast cancer. However, patients with implant-based reconstruction who receive radiation therapy have a higher risk of capsular contracture, a complication in which scar tissue tightens around the implant. In more severe cases, it can cause breast pain, firmness, or distortion and may require additional surgery.
A Mayo Clinic study published in the International Journal of Radiation Oncology, Biology, Physics found that areas around the implant receiving both higher proton beam radiation doses and elevated linear energy transfer (LET) were associated with capsular contracture. LET measures how densely protons deposit energy as they travel through tissue. If validated in larger studies, the findings could help clinicians refine proton therapy plans to reduce the risk of this complication.
"Pencil beam scanning proton therapy can deliver precise doses of radiation for breast cancer while sparing healthy tissue and organs in the chest," says Wei Liu, Ph.D., research director of medical physics at Mayo Clinic in Arizona and co-senior author of the study. "These findings give us a possible direction for making an already precise treatment even safer."
The retrospective study reviewed data from 145 patients at Mayo Clinic who received pencil beam scanning proton therapy for breast cancer. Eight patients developed clinically significant capsular contracture. Researchers compared their treatment plans with those of 16 carefully matched patients who did not develop the complication.
"We found that patients who developed capsular contracture tended to have more small areas where moderate or high radiation doses overlapped with elevated LET," says Dr. Liu. "Our findings suggest that it may not be enough to evaluate radiation dose or LET separately during radiation therapy planning, but rather the combination and overlap should be considered."
The research is part of the Mayo Clinic Comprehensive Cancer Center's Novel Therapeutics and Therapeutic Modalities Research Program, which includes research on proton therapy and strategies to reduce treatment toxicity. Dr. Liu is a member of the program. Robert Mutter, M.D., a breast radiation oncologist at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, and co-senior author of the study, co-leads the program.
"Proton therapy gives us extraordinary control over where radiation dose is deposited, but dose alone may not tell the whole story," says Dr. Mutter. "At Mayo Clinic, we routinely consider linear energy transfer when designing proton treatment plans, particularly where beams stop near sensitive normal tissues. These findings reinforce the importance of considering dose and LET together and may help us refine how we optimize proton therapy moving forward."
Next, the research team plans to validate the findings in larger groups of patients across multiple institutions and further evaluate the dose-LET relationships identified in this study. The team also will investigate whether incorporating LET into proton treatment planning can reduce normal tissue exposure to unfavorable combinations of dose and LET while preserving treatment effectiveness and sparing nearby organs.
For a complete list of authors, disclosures and funding, review the study.

Advances in radiation therapy allow doctors to target prostate cancer with increasing precision.
For a retired Navy pilot whose cancer had spread to his bones, that technology became part of a treatment plan aimed at giving him the best chance possible.
Watch: Precision radiation helps retired Navy pilot move forward after prostate cancer
Journalists: Broadcast-quality video (2:00) is in the downloads at the end of this post. Please courtesy: "Mayo Clinic News Network." Read the script.
"I'm retired," says Kevin Stewart. "I had a terrific career after 10 years as a Navy pilot. I was stationed on frigates, cruisers and destroyers. Anti-submarine warfare was my specialty."
Allison and Kevin Stewart while stationed in Hawaii.
But in 2021, Kevin noticed a change in his health.
"I experienced a sudden sense of urgency to urinate, and when I got to a position to try to urinate, I couldn't. It took quite a while, almost a year, for my stubbornness to ease and go to a doctor and describe it."
Kevin eventually saw a doctor near his home in St. Petersburg, Florida. A prostate-specific antigen (PSA) test came back elevated, prompting further evaluation.
"The first time he said I have cancer, I didn't hear anything after that," says Kevin.
The diagnosis was oligometastatic prostate cancer — meaning the cancer had spread beyond the prostate to areas in his bones. Through it all, Kevin leaned on his wife of 41 years, Allison Stewart.
"When you have a marriage or a partnership, and you say the vows and you know for better, for worse, sickness and health — Allison has demonstrated that there's meaning behind that," says Kevin.
Searching for opions
After three years of treatment, it became clear that he had not found a long-term solution.
"I think the first thing is you have to have a positive attitude," says Kevin. "The second thing you have to have is a partner. The third thing you have to have is you have to have a vision match with your care team. Your care team has to be on board with where you want to go and how you want to get there."
That search brought Kevin to Mayo Clinic in December 2025.
"I sat with him and his wife and just went through what our approach would be," says Dr. Albert Attia, a Mayo Clinic radiation oncologist. "We went over what we expect the outcome to be, that we're hoping to achieve a cure, although not promised, we want to give him the best chance possible."
Dr. Albert Attia with Kevin Stewart in June 2026.
The plan called for radiation therapy.
"Radiation works through several mechanisms, but one of the main ones is through DNA damage," explains Dr. Attia. "The cancer doesn't have very good repair mechanisms, and so when you damage the DNA of the cancer cells, they don't repair, and then they undergo cell death. We're also now discovering that radiation actually works also by ramping up the immune system and helping attack the cancer."
Targeted treatment
For Kevin, doctors used intensity-modulated radiation therapy, or IMRT, to precisely target the cancer.
"This is a way for us to shape the dose of radiation to deliver the high dose areas to the tumor and avoid any critical structures nearby," says Dr. Attia.
Kevin underwent 28 radiation treatments over six weeks, completing treatment in April 2026.
"By the end, you know, we're friends, and we're hugging. That was really gratifying and something I'll carry with me for the rest of my career," says Dr. Attia. "For me, it's an assurance that we're making strides, and we're really improving the lives of our patients."
"I feel great," Kevin says. "I have all of my energy back. They were expecting the initial PSA test of zero, and that's what we got."
Kevin and Allison Stewart visited Egypt in Sept. 2026
Returning to the life he planned
Kevin remains on hormone therapy and will continue regular follow-up with his radiation oncology team. Now, his focus is on returning to the life he and Allison had planned.
"It means we can get back to our lives," says Kevin. "We can go do the things we want to do that we spent a lifetime working to go do. In short, it means everything."

DEAR MAYO CLINIC: I'm finishing up treatment for lymphoma. I'm wondering what my life will be like after cancer. I don't know what the next steps will be. Can you help?
ANSWER: Finishing lymphoma cancer treatment is a major milestone, but the transition into survivorship can be challenging. During treatment, you have a routine. You may have chemotherapy every few weeks, meet with your care team and repeat that process over and over. Then, hopefully, you get the good news that you're in remission, and your scan looks great. Suddenly, that routine ends.
One of the most important things you can do is have a clear conversation with your care team about what happens next. Ask whether you'll need scans, how often you'll have follow-up visits and laboratory tests, and what symptoms you should watch for. Most lymphoma patients don't require ongoing scans, but regular follow-up visits, lab studies and physical exams may be part of your next steps.
Also, talk about how your cancer care will be coordinated with your primary care physician. Who will handle routine cancer screenings, such as mammograms or colonoscopies? How often should you see your primary care physician? Your care team can help you understand what follow-up makes sense for you.
How long does recovery from lymphoma treatment take?
Your recovery will depend in part on the type of lymphoma you've had and the treatment you received. There are more than 60 subtypes of lymphoma, and each behaves differently. Some are slow-growing lymphomas that can be treated and put into remission but are expected to return at some point. Others are aggressive diseases that may be curable with aggressive treatment.
For people who have been through intensive chemotherapy, a big part of recovery is regaining physical strength. There's also the mental and emotional aspect of processing the cancer experience, which often doesn't start happening until after treatment is over.
Fatigue is common, and it can take time to regain your energy. I tell people to think of their energy like a bank account. Maybe right now you have $100 worth of energy to spend each day. Over time, you may build that up to $150 or $200. But early on, you need to budget it. For example, if you have a big family event that may take most of your energy that day, rest beforehand and recover afterward.
Can exercise help after lymphoma treatment?
Physical activity should be part of that energy budget because it's been shown to improve quality of life and fatigue. Also, studies have found that being more physically active during survivorship is associated with a lower risk of lymphoma relapse. Physical activity comes in many different forms and should be something that you enjoy. An activity such as walking regularly and gradually working your way up can pay off in the long term.
Mind-body activities such as yoga also can help improve quality of life and fatigue. Choose the activity that suits you best, and you're more likely to stick with it.
Another common concern after treatment is peripheral neuropathy, which is the numbness and tingling in the fingers and toes caused by some chemotherapy drugs. It can be bothersome, but the majority of patients find it improves over time. Unfortunately, there isn't a magic pill to make it disappear faster, so recovery can require patience.
How can I cope with fear of lymphoma returning?
For many survivors, the No. 1 concern is the possibility that lymphoma will return. It's important to find a balance between appropriately watching for symptoms and learning to live comfortably with uncertainty. Talking about those feelings can help, whether that's with family and friends or with someone who has been through a similar experience. If anxiety or depression becomes overwhelming, don't hesitate to seek help from a mental health professional.
It also helps to recognize that life may not go back to exactly the way it was before lymphoma. You've been through a major life experience. I encourage people to find and embrace their "new normal" and to be patient and kind with themselves during early survivorship.
Finding your new normal after lymphoma
That new normal doesn't have to be about what you've lost. People can experience what's called post-traumatic growth — positive changes that can occur after lymphoma or another traumatic event. People may find that relationships become stronger, reconsider what matters most to them, make career changes, or prioritize their physical, mental, emotional and spiritual health differently.
Your cancer happened. But ask yourself: What helped me through this? What didn’t? What do I want for myself and my health moving forward?
Survivorship can be physically and emotionally challenging, but it also can be a beautiful time, an opportunity to celebrate the successes of treatment, embrace your new normal and make changes that help you live the best life you can. Join the conversation in the Mayo Clinic Connect Blood Cancers & Disorders Support Group.
Carrie Thompson, M.D., Hematology, Mayo Clinic Comprehensive Cancer Center, Rochester, Minnesota

The post Mayo Clinic Minute: Surgical advances help preserve function after stomach cancer treatment appeared first on Mayo Clinic News Network. ]]> Stomach cancer, also called gastric cancer, begins when cells grow abnormally in the stomach. More than 30,000 people in the U.S. are diagnosed with stomach cancer each year.
When stomach cancer is found early and has not spread, treatment can sometimes cure it. For cancer that has grown through the stomach wall or spread to other parts of the body, treatments may focus on controlling the cancer, relieving symptoms and helping people live longer.
In this Mayo Clinic Minute, Dr. Travis Grotz, a surgical oncologist at Mayo Clinic Comprehensive Cancer Center, explains how surgical innovations can help patients preserve stomach function and quality of life.
Watch: The Mayo Clinic Minute
Journalists: Broadcast-quality video (1:07) is in the downloads at the end of this post. Please courtesy: "Mayo Clinic News Network." Read the script.
What happens during stomach cancer surgery?
Treatment depends on where the cancer is located in the stomach and its stage. Options may include chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy and surgery.
"Surgery involves removing all or part of the stomach, and that depends on the extent of the tumor in the stomach and the lymph nodes around the stomach," says Dr. Grotz.
The goal of surgery is to remove all the cancer. In some cases, that means removing the entire stomach in a procedure called a total gastrectomy. The surgeon then connects the esophagus to the small intestine so food can move through the digestive system.
"If patients need a total gastrectomy, what they've lost is their storage reservoir, so they're limited to eating very, very small meals frequently," says Dr. Grotz. "But what we can do is, we can recreate a new stomach out of their intestine. We call that a J-pouch, and that restores some of that capacity for patients to eat larger meals afterward. And so then when they recover, they can have more normal function in eating than if they didn't have that pouch."
For stomach cancer surgery, a J-pouch is made from the jejunum, a portion of the small intestine, and is therefore referred to as a jejunal J-pouch. The J-pouch technique is more commonly used in colorectal surgery, where a pouch similarly serves as a storage reservoir. With a jejunal J-pouch reconstruction after total gastrectomy, the surgeon folds a segment of jejunum into a J shape and connects it to itself, creating a larger reservoir before connecting it to the esophagus.
"Although less commonly used in stomach cancer surgery and technically demanding, at Mayo Clinic we routinely perform this specialized reconstruction, offering an additional option to select patients," says Dr. Grotz.
Can part of the stomach be preserved?
Mayo Clinic surgeons are also studying techniques that can preserve part of the stomach.
In many Western countries, including the U.S., stomach cancer often starts in the upper part of the stomach, near the esophagus, and may be more advanced when diagnosed.
"For a long time, we have saved the upper part of the stomach whenever there's a tumor in the lower part, but it's been more challenging to remove the upper part of the stomach and save the bottom," explains Dr. Grotz. "We adapted a surgical technique and have a lot of experience here at Mayo Clinic in removing all the cancer and saving that bottom part of the stomach to get the benefits of stomach preservation."
